summary: This document specifies the Host Identity Protocol version 2. HIP separates the identifier and locator roles of IP addresses, so communication continues across address changes. It uses a Diffie-Hellman key exchange and public key host identities.

plainLanguage.summary: Your name stays the same even if you move houses. HIP gives computers a lasting name that is separate from their changing address, so connections survive moves.

questions: how does the hip base exchange work
what is a host identity tag
subtitle: A key exchange that gives hosts a lasting cryptographic identity, separate from the IP addresses they move between.

tldr.problem: An IP address is used both as a routing label (a locator) and as the name of an endpoint (an identifier), so communication cannot cleanly survive an address change, and hosts cannot authenticate each other at the IP layer.
tldr.mechanism: Each host uses a public key as its Host Identity and a 128-bit hash of it, the Host Identity Tag, in packets. Two hosts run a four-packet base exchange (I1, R1, I2, R2) that combines a Diffie-Hellman key exchange, signatures and a cryptographic puzzle that keeps the Responder stateless until the Initiator has done some work.
tldr.outcome: The result is a HIP association with shared keys, usable with ESP for integrity protection and optional encryption. RFC 7401 obsoletes RFC 5201, is not interoperable with HIP version 1, and has been updated by RFC 8002 and RFC 9374.

today: RFC 7401 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5201 and has since been updated by RFC 8002 and RFC 9374. HIP version 2 is not interoperable with the HIP version 1 of RFC 5201.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) proposes an alternative to the dual use of IP addresses as locators (routing labels) and identifiers (host names for the endpoint). In HIP, the public key of a public/private key pair is the host identifier, and higher-layer protocols bind to it instead of to an IP address. Because the identifier is a key, changes to a host's set of IP addresses can be authenticated directly between hosts.

This memo specifies the base protocol, called the base exchange, which sets up an IP-layer context called a HIP association. It also defines the packet format and the procedures for updating and closing an association. Other parts of the architecture are in separate documents, such as using ESP as the transport format (RFC 7402), host mobility, DNS extensions and rendezvous.

Version 2 adds cryptographic agility, meaning the ability to move from one algorithm to another, while addressing the downgrade attacks that such flexibility brings. It also adds elliptic curve support via ECDSA and ECDH. The RFC is explicit that HIP is not a complete replacement for IKE, because it does not cover IKE's fine-grained gateway policy control.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now your computer's address is both its name and its location, like using your home address as your name. HIP gives it a proper name that stays the same when it moves.

sections.title: Host Identity and Host Identity Tag
sections.content:
The Host Identity (HI) is the public key of an asymmetric key pair, and the host is the entity that holds the private key. Implementations MUST support RSA and ECDSA for generating the HI. Since keys vary in type and length, the HI is hashed into a fixed 128-bit Host Identity Tag (HIT). The HIT has the length of an IPv6 address, is self-certifying (given a HIT it is computationally hard to find a matching key), and has a very low probability of collision.

A HIT is an ORCHID, as defined in RFC 7343: an IANA-assigned prefix, a four-bit encoding of the algorithms used, and a 96-bit hashed representation of the HI. A HIT Suite groups the signature algorithm, the hash function and the truncation. The suite is carried in the OGA ID field of the HIT, so a host can tell from another host's HIT whether it supports the needed algorithms.

HIs and HITs are not expected in every data packet. With ESP, for example, the SPI in the ESP header maps data packets to the right association.
sections.plainLanguage: Your key is like a very long signature. The HIT is a short nickname made from that signature, short enough to fit in the same space as an address, and nobody else can easily fake a nickname that matches your signature.

sections.title: The Four-Packet Base Exchange
sections.content:
The base exchange is a four-packet, SIGMA-compliant exchange between an Initiator and a Responder. The Initiator sends I1, a trigger packet carrying its HIT, the Responder's HIT if known, and a list of Diffie-Hellman group IDs it supports. The Responder replies with R1, which holds a puzzle, its Diffie-Hellman value, its Host Identity, lists of algorithms and a signature. The Initiator solves the puzzle and answers with I2, containing the solution, its own Diffie-Hellman value, its Host Identity (optionally encrypted) and a MAC and signature. The Responder checks everything and finishes with R2, signed and MACed. Data starts to flow after the fourth packet.

The first two packets agree on the algorithms. The Diffie-Hellman exchange happens in the second and third packets, and authentication in the third and fourth. The roles of Initiator and Responder are typically forgotten once the exchange completes.

If the Initiator does not know the Responder's HIT, it can try opportunistic mode by putting all zeros in the destination HIT. The RFC is candid that this is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle on the path, since the Initiator has no key for the peer, but argues it is at least as secure as unprotected IP communication.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a four-step secret handshake. Knock, get a riddle, answer the riddle and show your ID, then get a final confirmation. After that the two of you share a secret code.

sections.title: The Puzzle and Denial-of-Service Defence
sections.content:
The puzzle exists to protect the Responder from denial-of-service attacks. The Responder supplies a random number #I and a difficulty #K. The Initiator must find a number #J such that the lowest-order #K bits of a hash over #I, the two HITs and #J are zero. The Responder can verify the answer by computing one hash, before it creates any state and before the costly signature checks and Diffie-Hellman work.

Because the puzzle is not covered by the R1 signature, the Responder can precompute and sign R1 packets and fill in the puzzle just before sending. The Responder can vary the difficulty by trust or load: values of #K that are too high exclude weak devices, and if the Responder is not under high load #K SHOULD be 0. The puzzle #I must not be guessable and the Responder must be able to tell that it chose it, and the secret behind this SHOULD be changed every few minutes.

Replays are handled by several mechanisms. Responders are protected from replayed I1 packets by answering statelessly with pre-signed R1s. Initiators are protected from replayed R1s by a monotonically increasing 64-bit R1 generation counter. The protocol designers deliberately chose not to put a timestamp in R1, to avoid needing global time synchronisation, and chose not to use a memory-bound puzzle function.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the server spends effort on you, it hands you a small homework problem. Checking your answer is quick for the server but takes you a little time, so a crowd of fakers cannot overwhelm it.

sections.title: Negotiation, Downgrade Protection and Keys
sections.content:
The Initiator lists its preferred Diffie-Hellman groups in the I1, in a DH_GROUP_LIST. The I1 is deliberately not signed, to avoid costly work on floods of I1 packets, so that list could be tampered with. The Responder therefore chooses the first group in its own list that the Initiator also supports and returns its own list in the signed part of the R1. The Initiator continues only if the group in the R1 is the most preferred one supported by both. Otherwise it treats the exchange as a downgrade attack and MUST restart or abort. If the Initiator's HIT Suite is not in the Responder's list, it can abort or restart with a suitable source HIT.

Key material, called KEYMAT, comes from the Diffie-Hellman shared secret run through the key derivation function that the group ID selects, which in this document is HKDF with the Responder's hash. The salt is #I and #J, and the HITs are sorted so both sides compute the same result. Four initial keys are drawn: an encryption key and an HMAC key for each direction. The Initiator can already encrypt its Host Identity in the I2 because it has the shared secret when it builds that packet.

Cipher choices for the encrypted parameter follow the same pattern: the Responder offers up to six, the Initiator picks one, and AES-128-CBC is the mandatory one. The NULL cipher is for testing and debugging only.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people agree on a secret language by each saying which ones they know. Because a trickster could whisper lies in the first message, the second message repeats the list in a way that cannot be changed, so cheating is noticed.

sections.title: HIP Packets and Parameters
sections.content:
Every HIP packet starts with a fixed 40-byte header: next header, header length, packet type, a four-bit version (2 for this document), a checksum, controls, and the sender's and receiver's HITs. The header is logically an IPv6 extension header, and this document only describes the next-header value 59, the IPv6 'no next header' value. IANA assigned protocol number 139 to HIP. Header Length counts 8-byte units excluding the first 8 bytes, so the parameters field can be at most 2008 bytes.

After the header come parameters in TLV format. They MUST appear in increasing numeric type order, and a packet that breaks this is malformed and MUST be discarded. Each parameter's total length is a multiple of 8 bytes, padded with zeros. The lowest bit of the type is the Critical bit: odd types are critical and MUST be recognised, or the packet is not processed further, while even types MAY be ignored if unknown.

The same packet family also carries UPDATE, which has a sequence number and explicit acknowledgment and is protected by both a MAC and a signature, plus NOTIFY for informational errors, and the CLOSE and CLOSE_ACK pair that signals the end of an association. Problems with no existing association can be reported with rate-limited ICMP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Every HIP message begins with the same header, like the top of a form with sender and receiver. After it come labelled boxes of information that must be placed in the right order.

sections.title: The HIP State Machine
sections.content:
HIP itself has little state. The state machine is symmetric, shown from the view of either an Initiator or a Responder, and the RFC calls it informational: implementations may process things differently, and the packet processing rules in Section 6 are what count. The states are UNASSOCIATED, I1-SENT, I2-SENT, R2-SENT, ESTABLISHED, CLOSING, CLOSED and E-FAILED.

Compared with RFC 5201, there is a new transition from I1-SENT back to I1-SENT, a restart for when the Responder does not support the Initiator's HIT Suite. The design is also meant to recover when one side crashes and loses its state. An Initiator that has lost state simply starts a new exchange, and the peer does not reset its state until it receives a valid I2.
sections.plainLanguage: The state machine is a board game: you start in one square and each message you send or get moves you to the next square, until you reach the one that means the connection is up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
HIP is designed to authenticate hosts and limit exposure to DoS and man-in-the-middle attacks, yet it is subject to its own such attacks. The RFC walks through several. Spoofed I1 packets can trick the Responder into sending large R1 packets at a victim, so the Responder SHOULD rate-limit R1 sending. Spoofed I1 can also make an Initiator waste work on an R1 it never asked for, which is why an Initiator ignores R1s without a matching I1.

Floods of forged I2 packets are limited by dropping solutions that repeatedly appear in bad packets, and an attacker has to solve puzzles to get on that list. Emulating a reboot or a CLOSE is blunted because CLOSE and CLOSE_ACK carry a MAC an outsider cannot forge. Replayed R1s are covered by the generation counter.

Man-in-the-middle attacks are hard to defend against without third-party authentication. If the Responder's HI is obtained from a signed DNS zone, a certificate or another secure means, the Initiator can use it to validate the R1. The RFC also warns that an eavesdropper who already knows the parties can identify them by HIT, so encrypting the HI does not give privacy against that attacker.

Reusing a Diffie-Hellman value under an I1 storm is allowed but discouraged, because it raises the risk of shared keying material and weakens forward secrecy.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad guys can try to make the server work too hard, or trick two computers into talking to a fake. HIP adds many small checks so most tricks fail early and cheaply.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH REPLAY OR DOS MECHANISM PROTECTS

items.title: Stateless R1
items.text: Protects Responders from replayed I1 packets.

items.title: R1 counter
items.text: A monotonically increasing 64-bit counter protects Initiators from replayed R1s.

items.title: Puzzle
items.text: Protects Responders from forged I2 floods before state or signature work.

items.title: MAC before signature
items.text: Protects hosts from replayed R2 and UPDATE packets at lower cost.

fields.desc: In 8-byte units, excluding the first 8 bytes; minimum is 4.
Fixed bit reserved for SHIM6 compatibility.

fields.name: Packet Type
fields.desc: Identifies I1, R1, I2, R2, UPDATE and so on.

fields.name: RES.
fields.desc: Reserved; zero when sent, ignored when received.
Fixed bit reserved for SHIM6 compatibility.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Covers a pseudo header with the IP addresses, so HIP-aware NATs must recompute it.

fields.name: Controls
fields.desc: Only the Anonymous bit is defined.

fields.name: Sender's HIT
fields.desc: 128-bit Host Identity Tag of the sender.

fields.name: Receiver's HIT
fields.desc: 128-bit Host Identity Tag of the receiver.
